# Chapter 7 — Nothing Can Be Decommissioned Without a Map

*The Dependency Mapping Requirement.*

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
The most dangerous moment in modernization is *decommissioning*, not
migration — it removes the safety net, and the failures are often silent.
This chapter catalogs the web of dependencies Active Directory accumulates and
establishes the requirement for a machine-readable, bidirectionally queryable
**dependency map** as a governance prerequisite.
:::

## The Most Dangerous Moment Is Not Migration

Infrastructure modernization programs are typically planned and communicated as migration programs. The framing is about moving things from one platform to another: moving workloads from on-premises servers to cloud infrastructure, moving identities from on-premises directories to cloud directories, moving device management from Group Policy to cloud-based management platforms. Migration receives the planning attention, the project resources, and the governance focus, because migration is the visible work — it has milestones, deliverables, and cutover dates that make it trackable and reportable.

But the most dangerous moment in any infrastructure modernization program is not the moment of migration. It is the moment of decommissioning. Migrating a workload to a new platform is recoverable — if the migration is incomplete or incorrect, the old platform is still available to fall back on, and the window for correction exists as long as the old infrastructure is running. Decommissioning the old platform eliminates that safety net. When the on-premises domain controllers are shut down, when the DNS zones are deleted, when the certificate authority infrastructure is taken offline, anything that was still depending on that infrastructure fails. And the critical condition that makes decommissioning dangerous is that the failures may not be immediately visible. A service that relied on LDAP directory queries and receives no response when the domain controllers are gone may fail silently, logging errors that go unnoticed for hours or days. An application that used NTLM authentication as a fallback when Kerberos failed may stop serving requests for a user population whose Kerberos tickets cannot be refreshed, with no obvious connection to the infrastructure decommissioning event that caused the failure.

## The Web of Dependencies That Active Directory Creates

Active Directory does not merely store identity information. It is the foundation of an enormous web of dependencies that accumulates over the operational life of the directory. Domain controllers are referenced by SRV records in DNS, and every domain-joined machine queries those records on a regular basis. Kerberos authentication for every application that uses integrated Windows authentication depends on those domain controllers being reachable and the domain being valid. LDAP bind operations from directory-aware applications — HR systems, ERP platforms, custom web applications, monitoring tools, backup software — depend on the domain controllers and the schema they serve. Group Policy processing for every domain-joined computer depends on domain controller reachability and SYSVOL access over SMB. Certificate enrollment for machines and users depends on the Certificate Authority infrastructure published in the Active Directory Certificate Services enrollment service records. NTLMv2 authentication falls back to domain controllers when Kerberos fails, and Kerberos fails in more circumstances than most architecture documentation acknowledges. Print spoolers, scheduled tasks running under domain service account identities, COM+ application identities, and legacy service wrappers all carry domain references that are embedded in configuration files, registry entries, and application databases that no centralized inventory has ever captured.

None of these dependencies are enumerated in any single Microsoft native tool. Active Directory itself does not maintain a dependency graph of what consumes it. The closest analogs — network traffic analysis, application inventory tools, and change management databases — each capture partial pictures from their own perspective. Network traffic analysis can identify LDAP query sources and Kerberos ticket requests, but it cannot identify what application logic those queries serve or what would happen if the queries returned no response. Application inventory tools can enumerate installed software but cannot identify the authentication mechanisms those applications use or the directory services they depend on. Change management databases record what was changed and when, but not what depends on what. The complete dependency picture must be assembled from multiple partial views, and the assembly process is manual, incomplete, and time-consuming — which means it is typically performed under pressure, as decommissioning deadlines approach, rather than methodically, as a prerequisite to planning.

## The Map as a Governance Prerequisite

The requirement this situation establishes is unambiguous. Before any Active Directory dependency — any domain controller, any DNS zone, any certificate authority, any domain-joined computer — can be decommissioned, a complete dependency map must exist that identifies every consumer of that dependency, the nature of the dependency, and the migration target for each consumer. The dependency map is not a project planning artifact. It is a governance prerequisite. An organization that decommissions infrastructure without a complete, current dependency map is not making an informed governance decision — it is accepting unknown risk that will materialize as service failures affecting users and applications whose migration status was unknown at the time of decommissioning.

The dependency map must be machine-readable, meaning it must exist as a structured data artifact that can be queried programmatically, not as a spreadsheet maintained by a project team member or a diagram in a presentation. It must be continuously updated as the environment changes — as new applications are deployed, as new servers are enrolled, as existing dependencies are migrated and resolved. And it must be queryable in both directions: given an infrastructure component, the map must return every consumer of that component; given a consumer, the map must return every infrastructure dependency it holds. This bidirectional queryability is what makes the map useful for migration planning, for decommissioning risk assessment, and for incident response when a dependency failure occurs unexpectedly.

::: {.callout-note title="Architectural Requirement — Chapter 7"}
Before any Active Directory dependency can be decommissioned, a complete, machine-readable dependency map must exist that identifies every consumer of that dependency, the nature of the dependency, and the migration target for each consumer. The dependency map must be continuously updated as the environment changes and must be queryable in both directions — from component to consumers and from consumer to dependencies. The map must be maintained as a governance artifact, not reconstructed from memory or inferred from network traffic at the moment of planned decommissioning.
:::
